One-sentence verdict: this line of work is not "assembling PCs" or "fixing computers"; it is researching, designing, developing or testing computer and computer-related equipment for commercial, industrial, military or scientific use, and possibly supervising their manufacture and installation. O*NET defines the occupation as "research, design, develop, or test computer or computer-related equipment for commercial, industrial, military, or scientific use; may supervise the manufacturing and installation of computer or computer-related equipment and components," and its tasks rank "update knowledge and skills to keep up with rapid advancements in computer technology" and "design and develop computer hardware and support peripherals, including central processing units, support logic, microprocessors, custom integrated circuits, printers and disk drives" as the top two; this page follows the exact occupational scope of O*NET-SOC 17-2061.00.

Signals for exploring further: you are willing to write "performance and interface constraints" as testable metrics, and you accept that a design only counts once it has been through prototypes and test data. O*NET work context shows 93% use email every day, 76% work more than 40 hours per week (24% at 40 hours), 79% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day, 61% sit continuously or almost continuously (29% more than half the time), 59% consider being very exact or highly accurate extremely important (31% very important), 43% consider work with a work group or team extremely important (50% very important), 50% have face-to-face discussions every day (46% more than once a week), 31% have a great deal of decision freedom (66% some freedom), 21% have a great deal of freedom to determine tasks and priorities (66% some freedom), 19% consider competition extremely intense (59% very intense, 19% moderate), 36% consider the consequences of error serious (14% very serious, 21% fairly serious), 39% of the work is moderately automated (39% slight, 18% high), 86% stand less than half the time, 59% need to walk or run less than half the time, 78% never come into contact with minor burns or cuts, 96% never come into contact with disease or infection, and 93% never come into contact with radiation.

Conditions for pausing before heavy investment: you have not yet completed one full loop of "requirements and specification confirmation — architecture and interface design — prototype implementation — testing and verification — problem localization and iteration — documentation and handover," and you have not verified your employer's mandatory requirements for design review, component compliance (such as electrostatic discharge protection and reliability), and test data and intellectual property ownership. This occupation's preparation level is Job Zone Four (considerable preparation), the page's education distribution is expressed as "most positions require a four-year bachelor's degree, some do not," and the SVP range is 7.0 to 8.0; the occupation page marks this code as Bright Outlook, but this page does not infer individual hiring probability from that.

Education, on-the-job training, professional certifications, licenses and job authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (considerable preparation), the page's education distribution is expressed as "most positions require a four-year bachelor's degree, some do not," and the SVP range is 7.0 to 8.0; the page also provides 12 national certifications (such as Robotics Certification, Certified TestStand Architect, Certified Reliability Engineer, Registered Communications Distribution Designer, Fundamentals of Engineering - Electrical and Computer, ESD (Electrostatic Discharge) Associate Engineer, among others), and the page also lists 1 registered apprenticeship example (Hardware Engineer); but a certification or apprenticeship experience is not equal to a degree, an employer appointment, design signing authority or product certification qualification; component and product safety and electromagnetic compatibility and reliability compliance, and the management of technical materials subject to export control, must be confirmed item by item according to the applicable jurisdiction and employer and customer policy; this page describes tasks and boundaries based on O*NET and public sources, and does not present education or certifications as statutory qualifications.

In one sentence: this is an occupation in which "defining the metrics accurately, being able to build the prototype, and explaining the test data clearly" are all indispensable; whether the design passes review, whether the prototype meets the specification, and whether problems can be traced to root cause determine whether your solution is adopted. If you are willing to live with constraints over the long term and accept repeated iteration, it is worth serious consideration.

The work of Computer Hardware Engineers can be divided into three connected but distinct work areas. The first is requirements and architecture and design: confer with engineering staff and review specifications to evaluate the interface between hardware and software and the operational and performance requirements of the overall system; design and develop computer hardware and support peripherals, including central processing units (CPUs), support logic, microprocessors, custom integrated circuits and printers and disk drives; select hardware and materials and ensure they meet specifications and product requirements; evaluate factors such as reporting formats required, cost constraints and safety restrictions to determine hardware configuration; and specify power supply requirements and configuration based on system performance expectations and design specifications. The second is prototypes and testing and verification: build, test and modify product prototypes using working or theoretical models constructed with computer simulation; test and verify hardware and support peripherals by recording and analyzing test data to ensure they meet specifications and requirements; store, retrieve and manipulate data to analyze system capabilities and requirements; and analyze information to determine, recommend and plan layout, including the type and modification of computers and peripherals. The third is documentation and collaboration and technical support: write detailed functional specifications that document the hardware development process and support hardware introduction; provide technical support to designers and marketing and sales departments and suppliers and engineers and other team members throughout the product development and implementation process; direct technicians and engineering design staff or other technical support personnel; provide training and support to system designers and users; monitor equipment functioning and make necessary modifications to ensure the system operates to specifications; recommend purchase of equipment to control dust and temperature and humidity in the area where a system is installed; and assemble and modify existing equipment to meet special needs.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether requirements and specifications are written to a testable degree; whether interfaces and assumptions are explicit and have been reviewed; whether simulation and testing cover boundary and failure cases; whether test data and versions are reproducible; whether components and materials meet specification and compliance requirements; and whether design and test documentation is complete with handover finished.
Check one: are requirements and specifications written to a testable degree

Turn requirements into measurable metrics (bandwidth, latency, power, temperature range, reliability and cost); state assumptions and verification methods for parts that cannot be quantified; do not substitute unquantified statements such as "better performance" for testable acceptance conditions.
Check two: are interfaces and assumptions explicit and have they been reviewed

Write the interface, timing and electrical characteristics between hardware and software into documents and review them; make external dependencies and uncontrollable conditions explicit and flag the risk; review interface changes through the procedure and update the version of the relevant documents.
Check three: do simulation and testing cover boundary and failure cases

Cover upper and lower limits and abnormal and failure combinations in addition to nominal conditions; record the differences between simulation and measurement and explain the reasons; explicitly write the risk and follow-up verification plan for scenarios not yet covered.
Check four: are test data and versions reproducible

Record the test conditions and environment and instruments and firmware and versions and sample numbers; retain the raw data and processing scripts; enable others to reproduce the same conclusion from the records, rather than seeing only the conclusion charts.
Check five: do components and materials meet specification and compliance requirements

Verify the datasheet and temperature and lifetime and certification status when selecting parts; verify substitute parts and retain comparison data; handle materials and materials subject to safety and electromagnetic compatibility and export control according to employer and customer policy.
Check six: is design and test documentation complete with handover finished

Archive functional specifications and design change records and test reports by version; write known issues and limitations and follow-up plans into the handover materials; document the support and training after handover.

The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: reading specifications and drawings, turning requirements into metrics, arguing from test data, and communicating with cross-departmental teams. The real difference lies in the object and the acceptance method: this occupation centers on the hardware design and verification of computers and computer-related equipment; the systems analysis direction is mainly business solutions; the systems architecture direction is mainly whole-machine and system coordination; the electrical and electronics directions have different objects; the radio frequency identification direction focuses on tag and reader systems; and the research science direction is mainly about new principles and methods, without mass-producibility as a constraint. When choosing, it is advisable to first validate with one deliverable exercise in "specifications and metrics — interface definition — test plan and data," rather than comparing titles first.

The comparison basis is the occupational definition and the 18 tasks and work activities and work context descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 17-2061.00 page, the related occupations and adjacent occupation codes listed on that page, the adjacent occupation slug list registered in this evidence route (computer-systems-analysts, computer-systems-engineers-architects, electrical-engineers, electronics-engineers-except-computer, radio-frequency-identification-device-specialists), and the public occupational materials for each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial compilation and does not constitute engineering safety, compliance or legal conclusions.

The table below compares the positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: computer systems analysts, computer systems engineers and architects, electrical engineers, electronics engineers (except computer), radio frequency identification device specialists and computer and information research scientists. The four columns each answer the same kind of question: what the direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

Computer systems analysts mainly translate business requirements into system solutions and coordinate them and usually do not carry hardware design and verification responsibility; this occupation has hardware metrics and test data as its acceptance object.
People willing to do requirements analysis and system solution coordination suit that direction; people willing to do hardware design and verification suit this occupation.
Mainly requirements and solutions and implementation coordination records.

Computer systems engineers and architects mainly handle system-level architecture and integration and performance and focus on whole-machine and system coordination; this occupation focuses on hardware design and verification at the chip and board and peripheral level.
People willing to do system-level architecture and integration suit that direction; people willing to go deep into hardware level suit this occupation.
Mainly system architecture and integration and performance records.

Electrical engineers work on power and electrical systems and equipment; this occupation works on the digital and analog hardware of computers and computer-related equipment, with performance and interface metrics as the acceptance object.
People willing to work on power and electrical systems suit that direction; people willing to do computing hardware design suit this occupation.
Mainly electrical system design and inspection records.

Electronics engineers (except computer) work on non-computer electronic devices and circuits and communications equipment; this occupation's object is limited to computers and computer-related equipment and components.
People willing to do general electronics and communications circuits suit that direction; people willing to do computing hardware suit this occupation.
Mainly electronic circuit and device and communications equipment records.
Electronics engineers (except computer)
Radio frequency identification device specialists mainly deploy and tune RFID tags and readers and systems; this occupation is responsible for broader computer hardware design and verification.
People willing to do RFID solution deployment and tuning suit that direction; people willing to do hardware design and verification suit this occupation.
Mainly RFID solution and deployment and tuning records.
Radio frequency identification device specialists

Computer and information research scientists mainly do basic research and the verification of new principles and new methods, with longer research cycles and no goal of guaranteeing mass production; this occupation works under the constraints of meeting specifications and manufacturability.
People willing to do long-term basic research suit that direction; people willing to deliver hardware designs under engineering constraints suit this occupation.
Mainly papers and methods and experiment records.
Computer and information research scientists

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires filling in new competencies and experience: the systems analysis direction requires business modeling and requirements engineering experience; the systems architecture direction requires whole-machine and integration and performance engineering experience; the electrical direction requires power and electrical system design and inspection experience; the electronics direction requires non-computer electronic device and communications circuit experience; the RFID direction requires tag and reader and field deployment experience; the research science direction requires research methods and papers and experiment records. Metric definition and test verification ability can transfer, but the object and acceptance method of each direction must be rebuilt.

First build solid foundations in circuits and digital systems, simulation and testing methods, and specification and interface writing, then learn to use generative tools to assist with material retrieval and code and scripts and documentation; do not treat tool output directly as a design conclusion or test evidence, and do not skip verification against measured data and datasheets.
Positions responsible for solutions and modeling

Use tools for material retrieval and design drafts and parameter sweep scripts and document organization, but keep metric definition, interface trade-offs and performance and cost trade-offs with yourself and the review, and be accountable for the accuracy and verifiability of citations and calculation bases.
Positions responsible for prototypes and testing

Editor's suggestion: trial test scripts, data and report drafts in permitted and verified tools; test conditions, failure criteria and measurement uncertainty are checked by engineering staff, and the environment, instruments, firmware, versions and raw data are retained.
Positions responsible for documentation and compliance and delivery

State the test conditions and samples and instruments and period clearly, annotate the applicable scope of the conclusions and retain the raw data, and have verification conclusions confirmed by review.

paragraphs: The six cards below are editorial risk scenarios and control suggestions proposed on the basis of the U.S. O*NET tasks, not accident frequencies, incidence rates or verified enterprise procedures. Specific product regulations, test authorization and confidentiality policy must be verified separately; this page obtained no specific product/jurisdiction compliance text.

Editorial judgment: first verify whether the specifications and interfaces are testable, whether verification covers the applicable boundaries, and whether version data is reproducible; failure and rework are possible consequences, and this round has no evidence ranking the three risk types as most necessary or most common.

The occupational tasks/context are U.S. O*NET17-2061; for the nine sections employment uses 2025—2035 and wages use 2025. The Chinese industry reference and the precise occupational gap are listed separately. Compliance/export control/confidentiality are only flagged as requiring verification against the actual product, destination, entity and policy, and are not a legal conclusion that all components must be certified.
Positions responsible for requirements and specifications and architecture design
If specifications and metrics are not written to a testable level, the design will be reworked repeatedly and failures will be exposed at the review and volume-production introduction stages.

Turn requirements into measurable metrics and define test methods; state assumptions and verification methods for parts that cannot be quantified; check performance and power and cost and manufacturability constraints together during the architecture review.
Substituting context-free statements such as "better performance" for metrics; entering implementation without an architecture review; adding explanations of constraints only afterwards.
Positions responsible for interfaces and component selection
Hardware and software interfaces or third-party components or substitute parts that are not verified will cause integration failure or batch failures and affect delivery and warranty.

Write the interface and timing and electrical characteristics into documents and review them; verify third-party components and substitute parts and retain comparison and batch data; establish qualified supplier and change review mechanisms for critical materials.
Verifying interfaces only under nominal conditions; putting unverified substitute parts directly into volume production; not recording component batch differences.
Positions responsible for prototypes and test verification
Testing that covers only nominal conditions or does not cover failure combinations postpones the current problem to volume production and customer sites and amplifies recall and reputation risk.

Cover upper and lower limits and abnormal and failure combinations per the test plan; record the test conditions and environment and instruments and firmware and versions and sample numbers; write the risk and a follow-up verification plan for uncovered scenarios.
Doing only "it powers on" level verification; not recording test conditions and instrument settings; modifying the design on abnormal results without tracing root cause.
Positions responsible for data and documentation and versions
Design and test data that is not versioned or not reproducible means the review cannot check the conclusion, and customer complaints and compliance audits cannot be traced.

Retain raw data and processing scripts and version records; enable others to reproduce the same conclusion from the records; archive functional specifications and design changes and test reports by version and complete the handover.
Keeping only conclusion charts; managing versions with personal naming habits; giving only oral explanations at handover without delivering materials.
Positions responsible for compliance and material management

Unconfirmed component and product safety and electromagnetic compatibility and reliability compliance, or improper management of technical materials subject to export control, brings compliance liability and external cooperation risk.

Editor's suggestion: have personnel designated by the organization verify the applicable safety, electromagnetic compatibility and reliability requirements and documents for the specific market/product; verify classification, destination, recipient and license for potentially controlled materials, and disclose according to confirmed authorization. Insufficient evidence: this page obtained no original text of a specific product certification or export list.

Adopting substitute parts without verification or without meeting applicable compliance requirements; uploading controlled materials to unauthorized external channels; making external technical commitments before organizational approval. Not every uncertified component is in itself unlawful.
Positions responsible for design changes and handover
Design changes that are not reviewed or not synchronized to manufacturing and support cause version mismatches and rework on the production line and at suppliers.

Review changes per procedure and update specifications and drawings and test plans and bills of materials in step; write known issues and limitations and follow-up plans into the handover materials; document the support and training after handover.
Announcing changes orally; changing only the document and not the bill of materials; not keeping a traceable issue list after handover.

entries.answer: Daily work is mainly requirements and architecture and design, prototyping and testing and validation, documentation and collaboration and technical support: discussing with engineers and consulting specifications to assess hardware and software interfaces and system performance requirements; designing and developing computer hardware and supporting peripherals (including CPU and support logic and microprocessors and custom integrated circuits); selecting hardware and materials and ensuring they meet specifications; building and testing and modifying product prototypes using working models or theoretical models; recording and analyzing test data to verify whether hardware and peripherals meet specifications; writing functional specifications and documenting the hardware development process; providing technical support to designers and marketing and sales and suppliers; instructing technicians and training users; and monitoring equipment function and making necessary modifications. The work context shown on this page: 93% use email every day, 50% have face-to-face discussions every day, 61% sit continuously or almost continuously, and 59% consider being very exact or highly accurate extremely important.
entries.question: What does a computer hardware engineer do every day?

entries.answer: Computer systems analysts focus on translating business requirements into system solutions and coordinating them; computer systems engineers and architects focus on system-level architecture and integration and performance; electrical engineers work on power and electrical systems and equipment; electronics engineers (except computer) work on non-computer electronic components and communications equipment; radio frequency identification device specialists focus on deploying and tuning RFID tags and readers and systems; computer and information research scientists focus on basic research and new principles and new methods. This occupation centers on the hardware design and development and test validation of computers and computer-related equipment. Shared capabilities do not mean the roles are interchangeable: the objects and acceptance methods differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between this occupation and adjacent occupations?

entries.answer: It cannot be inferred that way. The core tasks of this occupation include setting metrics and constraints, making interface and architecture trade-offs, prototyping and test validation, and design change and delivery responsibility; these steps depend on engineering training and review and authority. In addition, the ILO exposure index registered in this evidence route is only a task exposure measure, not a replacement rate or job reduction forecast. The more reliable uses of tools are information retrieval and design drafts and scripts and document drafts.

entries.answer: From the task structure, the earlier-affected parts are the structurable and digitizable steps: specification and information retrieval and comparison, design drafts and script and template generation, test data processing and charts, and document and specification drafts. The later-affected parts are the steps requiring judgment and responsibility: setting metrics and constraints, interfaces and architecture and trade-offs, prototype and measured validation and failure criteria, and design change and compliance and external disclosure. It must be stressed that this judgment is editorial synthesis, not an exposure measure or job forecast provided by a source.

entries.answer: Converging requirements into measurable and verifiable metrics, making trade-offs among performance and power and cost and manufacturability and bearing the consequences, judging whether tests cover real failure cases, and completing compliance and confidentiality and disclosure per the system. description.text: Computer hardware engineers research, design, develop or test computer and computer-related equipment for commercial and industrial and military or scientific use, centered on requirements and architecture and design, prototyping and testing and validation, and documentation and collaboration and technical support: 18 tasks and the work context, the U.S. BLS 2025 median wage of 161,740 USD and 2024—2034 growth of 7%, the registered Mainland China wage gap and the handling of publishing no values, entry and qualification and authority paths, and compliance and export control and confidentiality boundaries and the exercise, all in one view.

subject.name: Computer hardware engineer
subject.summary: Research, design, develop or test computer and computer-related equipment for commercial, industrial, military or scientific use, and possibly supervise its manufacture and installation: discuss with engineers and consult specifications to assess hardware and software interfaces and system operation and performance requirements; design and develop computer hardware and supporting peripherals, including central processing units and support logic and microprocessors and custom integrated circuits and printers and disk drives; select hardware and materials and ensure they meet specifications and product requirements; evaluate cost and safety and reporting format requirements to determine hardware configuration; specify power supply requirements and configuration; build and test and modify product prototypes using working models built through computer simulation or theoretical models; test and validate hardware and supporting peripherals by recording and analyzing test data; write detailed functional specifications and document the hardware development process; provide technical support to designers and marketing and sales and suppliers and engineers; instruct technicians and engineering design staff; provide training and support to system designers and users; and monitor equipment function and make necessary modifications.
